lesson_title: Crates and Loose Bottles: Simplifying Algebraic Fractions
hook_text: You cannot cancel that x. Here is the spaza-shop reason why.
clip_script: Spaza shop stockroom. Six crates of cooldrink on the counter, nine crates underneath. Six over nine — and because both piles are built out of nothing but crates, you shrink it honestly: divide both by three, two over three. Now change one thing. Six crates PLUS one loose bottle on top. Can you still chop out a crate? No — because the loose bottle belongs to no crate, and the moment you start chopping you have to explain what happens to it. That loose bottle is a plus sign. So here is the law: cancel only what the WHOLE top and the WHOLE bottom are built out of. Factorising is just the repacking job. x squared minus nine repacks into x minus three, times x plus three. x squared plus seven x plus twelve repacks into x plus three, times x plus four. Both piles have an x plus three crate — out it comes. Answer: x minus three over x plus four. And test it like a shopkeeper checks a till: put x equal to one in both. Minus two fifths, minus two fifths. Balanced. One last thing — the bottom may never be zero. You cannot share R240 among zero people.
visual_style: A bright spaza stockroom: stacked crates forming a fraction bar, one loose bottle glowing red beside a plus sign, crates lifting away as brackets cancel, a till slip printing the check.
pacing: Brisk counter-talk on the crates, a hard beat on the loose bottle, calm resolve on the till check.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and never lose a mark to an illegal cancel again.
